# RV power station and solar panel picks

For an RV, you want a unit with enough AC output for your biggest load, and a solar input high enough that your panels aren't throttled. Roof A/C needs roughly 1,500W running and over 3,000W at startup ([EmergencyEnergy](https://www.emergencyenergy.co/articles/rv-power-station/)). Most other loads (fridge, lights, laptop, Starlink) are small.

## My picks

**1. Best value, for boondocking without A/C: ALLPOWERS S2000 Pro + 400W solar kit**
- 1,451Wh, 2,400W output, with a 400W foldable panel.
- $963, or about $866.70 with code ALLPOWERS26 (tested in the brand's cart 2026-10-25).
- The 400W panel is a good match for this size of battery. A 300-400W array can refill a mid-size unit in a full day of decent sun ([EmergencyEnergy](https://www.emergencyenergy.co/articles/rv-power-station/)).
- [Buy the kit](https://dealectric.com/go/allpowers-s2000-pro-sp037-solar-kit)

**2. Best mid-range, for multi-day trips: BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 + 200W panel kit**
- 2,073.6Wh, 2,600W output.
- $1,199, or about $1,139.05 with code AFF5OFF (tested 2026-10-25).
- 200W of solar is on the light side for a 2kWh battery. Plan to add panels, or pair it with campground hookups.
- [Buy the kit](https://dealectric.com/go/bluetti-elite-200-v2-200w-solar-kit)

**3. If you want a built-in 30A RV outlet: BLUETTI AC200L**
- 2,048Wh, 2,400W, with up to 1,200W of solar input ([SmartEnergyEdge](https://smartenergyedge.com/best-portable-power-station-with-solar-panels-for-camping/)), and a 30A RV port ([EmergencyEnergy](https://www.emergencyenergy.co/articles/rv-power-station/)).
- $899, or about $854.05 with code AFF5OFF.
- It's sold without panels, so you'd add your own. The high solar input leaves room for a larger array.
- [Buy the AC200L](https://dealectric.com/go/bluetti-ac200l)

**4. Best for full-time RVing or running A/C: EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3**
- 4,096Wh, 4,000W continuous, and 8,000W surge. It can expand past 12kWh, and 0-80% wall recharge takes about 50 minutes.
- It's heavy (a two-person lift) and the priciest option once you add batteries. I don't have a current price or direct buy link in my results, so check the product details in [this review](https://www.emergencyenergy.co/articles/rv-power-station/) and compare retailers.
- The same review picks the Jackery Explorer 3000 Pro (3,024Wh, 3,000W) as a simpler option for A/C.

## Things to check
- **Solar input limit:** A big array is wasted if the unit caps input low. The Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 tops out at 400W, while the EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus accepts up to 1,000W ([SmartEnergyEdge](https://smartenergyedge.com/best-portable-power-station-with-solar-panels-for-camping/)).
- **Sizing:** Add up your watts times hours. A 150W fridge over 10 hours is about 1,500Wh ([Acquired Sense](https://www.acquiredsense.com/reviews/power-stations.html)).
- **Wiring:** Plugging in through a TT-30 adapter is fine. Anything hardwired into the RV should go through a licensed electrician.
- **Pricing:** The codes and prices above come from Dealectric, which earns a commission on its links. They were last checked 2026-10-25, so confirm the final price at checkout.

If you tell me what you run (A/C, fridge, CPAP, Starlink) and how many nights off-grid, I can narrow it to one pick.
